newsitem.title: USA: British defence chief holds Washington talks.
newsitem.headline: British defence chief holds Washington talks.

text.p: British Defence Secretary George Robertson discussed issues from Bosnia to NATO enlargement with U.S. officials on Tuesday and delivered a warm security message from Britain's new Labour government.
"We are a ... new goverment re-committed to the alliances with our neighbours and especially that trans-Atlantic relationship that has been so important to our country," he told reporters.
Robertson met Defence Secretary William Cohen and talked separately with leaders of Congress and White House National Security Adviser Sandy Berger.

Cohen and Robertson stressed in comments to reporters at the Pentagon that neither of their governments had made a final decision on how many former Soviet bloc states should be admitted to NATO in a western summit decision next month.
Cohen met earlier on Tuesday with visiting Slovenian Defence Minister Tit Turnsek, whose country is currently given a chance, along with Romania, of joining NATO.
The three leading candidates to be admitted to the alliance at a NATO summit meeting in Spain next month are the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.

Robertson and Cohen told a joint news conference that the current schedule for the NATO-led military stabilisation force (SFOR) to pull out of Bosnia by the end of next June would be kept and that leaders in the country should not count on a force to maintain peace beyond that date.

"From my perspective, the SFOR mission is supposed to end, will end, at the end of June '98. And we ought to do what we can to simply keep our focus on what needs to be done between now and then," Cohen said.

Cohen was pressed on the issue amid reports that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright would like to soften that firm stand against a pullout if such a move would result in new hostilities among former warring factions in Bosnia.

"I think it only undercuts our abilities to carry out that mission now to speculate on what could take place by any number of nations in the future," he responded when asked if U.S. and allied troops might be stationed near Bosnia instead of in the country after the pullout deadline.
"We went into Bosnia together; we are staying together and we will leave together. And that is the method that they (Bosnian officials) should not misunderstand," Robertson added.
"I think it's wrong to focus on June '98, when there is so much to be done at the present moment," he said.

Both said that not enough was being done in civilian efforts to rebuild Bosnia's infrastructure and repeated that formation of an international police force was under consideration for possible arrests of accused war criminals in Bosnia.
